260	## Step 4 — Build the flow **[T2]**
261	
262	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-build-scaffold-assumptions:start-->
263	> **`flow init` scaffolds ONLY the manual trigger (`start` / `core.trigger.manual`) with zero edges.** Every other user-owned node — **including the End node** — is yours to add via `Edit` / `Write`. Any HTTP / connector / connector-trigger node you `node add`-ed in T1 is already in `nodes[]` and `definitions[]` but has empty `inputs.detail` (filled in T3) and is not wired yet.
264	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-build-scaffold-assumptions:end-->
265	
266	### T2 batch — issue these in ONE assistant message
267	
268	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t2-read-source:start-->
269	1. **One `Read`** of `<ProjectName>.flow` — required before any Edit/Write; T1's chained Bash mutated the file and Claude Code's file-state tracker does not auto-refresh on external mutations.
270	<!--skill-flavor:greenfield-t2-read-source:end-->
271	2. **A batch of parallel `Edit` calls** — one per top-level array you're modifying. Same-file Edits serialize in execution order, so each `old_string` must anchor to text NO OTHER parallel Edit modifies. Use the **per-array anchor pattern** below.
272	   - Edit `nodes[]` — add the End node (and any other user-owned nodes).
273	   - Edit `definitions[]` — paste the End definition verbatim from T1's `registry get core.control.end` output.
274	   - Edit `edges[]` — wire `trigger → <httpNode> → end`. End-node `outputs` mapping goes here too if you declared an `out` variable in `variables.globals`.
275	   - Edit `layout.nodes` — placeholder `{ position: { x: 0, y: 0 }, size: { width: 96, height: 96 }, collapsed: false }` per new node; `format` rewrites both position and size (by node shape) in T3.
276	
277	   `Write` of the whole file is allowed but token-costly on flows >~10 nodes — only fall back to `Write` when ≥70% of nodes change AND the file is small (see [editing-operations.md — Tool Selection Ladder](editing-operations.md#tool-selection-ladder)). **Never `Write` a flow that already has connector / connector-trigger / managed-HTTP nodes** — the rewrite clobbers their CLI-owned `bindings[]` / `inputs.detail` (invisible to `flow validate`); `Edit` in place, or re-run `node configure` as the last write. See [CAPABILITY.md — Node ownership](../CAPABILITY.md#node-ownership--who-authors-the-node).
278	
279	#### Anchoring parallel `.flow` Edits — anchor on what you Read, not on key order
280	
281	> **Do not assume a top-level key order.** The CLI does not guarantee which keys are present or in what sequence — fixtures show `runtime` before `nodes` on one flow and absent on another, and `bindings` / `variables` / `solutionId` / `projectId` / `metadata` appear in varying positions. Any anchor of the form "closing `]` + the NEXT top-level key" is coupled to that ordering and will silently break across CLI versions or between flows. **Anchor on the target array's OWN key instead — you just `Read` the file at the top of T2, so anchor to text that read actually contains.**
282	
283	Anchor each Edit using its target array's own opening key, located in the text you just Read — not adjacency to a neighbor key. The catch: `"nodes": [` and `"edges": [` are NOT unique in the file. They recur **inside inline `definitions[]`** (an HTTP v2 / agent / subprocess definition embeds its own nested `nodes`/`edges`) **and inside any `subflows.<id>` block** (each subflow holds its own `nodes`/`edges`) — so even a small flow can carry several copies. The reliable, version-independent discriminator is **indentation: the top-level array sits at 2-space indent; every nested one is deeper.** `"definitions": [` and the top-level `"layout": {` appear once each, so they need no disambiguation.
284	
285	| Edit target | Anchor on (from the text you Read) | How to insert |
286	|---|---|---|
287	| Append to `nodes[]` | The **2-space-indented** `\n  "nodes": [` (the top-level array — deeper-indented `"nodes": ["` inside definitions do not match the two-leading-space prefix) plus the `start` node's opening `{ "id": "start"`. | Insert the new node object as the first element, immediately after the `[`: `\n    { new node JSON },`. Head-insertion keeps `old_string` clear of the array's closing `]`. |
288	| Append to `edges[]` | The **2-space-indented** `\n  "edges": [`. A newly generated scaffold commonly has `\n  "edges": []`; the 2-space prefix distinguishes it from nested `edges` arrays. | When empty, replace `\n  "edges": []` with `\n  "edges": [\n    { new edge JSON }\n  ]`. When non-empty, anchor through the first edge and insert the new edge as the first element. |
289	| Append to `definitions[]` | `"definitions": [` plus the first definition's opening bytes. Top-level `definitions[]` is the only one in the file, so this is reliably unique. | Insert the new definition right after the opening `[`, as the first element. Never anchor on whatever key follows `definitions` — that key varies (`runtime`, `bindings`, `variables`, `layout`, depending on CLI version and what the flow contains). |
290	| Add an entry to `layout.nodes` | `"layout": {\n    "nodes": {\n      "start":` — `start` is the always-present trigger and the first key under `layout.nodes` in newly generated flows. The top-level `"layout": {` is the only one. | `"layout":` + `"start":` jointly disambiguate. Insert `"<newId>": { ... },\n      ` before `"start":`. CLI-owned nodes added via `node add` already have a `layout.nodes` entry — only add entries for nodes you author by hand (e.g. End). |
291	
292	**Why head-insertion.** Inserting the new element right after the array's opening `[` means the `old_string` never includes the array's closing `]` — so it cannot collide with a closing `]` from a nested object (`form.sections[].fields[]`), and it never references a sibling top-level key whose position is not guaranteed. JSON array element order is not semantically significant for `nodes` / `edges` / `definitions`, so head vs. tail insertion is equivalent; `flow format` normalizes layout regardless.
293	
294	**Disjointness rule.** Two parallel Edits MUST anchor on DIFFERENT top-level arrays — nodes-Edit on the top-level `nodes[]`, edges-Edit on the top-level `edges[]`, definitions-Edit on `definitions[]`, layout-Edit on `layout.nodes`. Because each anchors on its own array (not a shared boundary), the parallel Edits never overlap — provided each anchor is unique first (see below).
295	
296	**Pre-flight uniqueness check.** Before submitting an Edit, confirm your `old_string` appears **exactly once** in the file you Read. `"definitions": [` and the top-level `"layout": {` are reliably unique. `"nodes": [` and `"edges": [` are NOT — they recur inside inline definitions and subflows, so anchor on the **2-space-indented** occurrence and extend through the first element's opening (e.g. `"id": "start"`) until the match count is one. Never anchor on a bare bracket shape, and never assume the first textual occurrence is the top-level one.
297	
298	**Safer fallback when in doubt:** serialize the Edits across two turns. One extra turn is cheaper than a failed-Edit recovery loop (which forces a re-Read, a re-derived anchor, and a re-submit).
299	
300	**Or skip the anchoring problem:** `scripts/flow_edit.py` and `scripts/flow_compose.py` parse the file and rewrite the arrays directly, so no `old_string` has to be unique. One call per node, edge, variable, or composite rewrite — see [editing-operations-json.md](editing-operations-json.md) for the per-operation flags. `Edit` remains the right tool for a small in-place value change you want to show as a diff.
301	
302	See [shared/file-format.md — Top-level structure](../../shared/file-format.md#top-level-structure) for which top-level keys exist and the note that their order is not guaranteed.
303	
304	> **Intra-turn ordering.** If a parallel `Edit` fails with "file not read," split `Read` into its own turn (cost: +1 turn).

3	The flow needs to pause for a human to review, approve, or fill in data. Two node types serve this need — choose based on form complexity and whether an app already exists.

5	---
6	
7	## Which HITL Node to Use
8	
9	| Use case | Node type | Form source |
10	| --- | --- | --- |
11	| Inline form designed right now (fields + outcomes defined in the flow) | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` | Schema embedded in node inputs — no app needed |
12	| Existing coded app or Action Center app | `uipath.human-in-the-loop.coded-action-app` | Deployed app from Orchestrator |
13	
14	**Prefer `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`** for new flows. It is an OOTB node — no registry discovery, no app publishing, no tenant dependency.

17	
18	## Option 1 — `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form` (Inline Schema — OOTB)
19	
20	Node type: `uipath.human-in-the-loop.quick-form`
21	Available: always — no `uip login` or registry pull required.
22	
23	### When to Select
24	
25	| Situation | Select? |
26	| --- | --- |
27	| Manager approval before processing | Yes |
28	| Human reviews extracted data before submission | Yes |
29	| Human resolves exceptions the automation cannot handle | Yes |
30	| Need a quick form with specific fields and outcomes | Yes |
31	| Existing coded/Action Center app should be used | No — use Option 2 |
32	| Fully automated processing, no human involvement | No |
33	
34	### Ports
35	
36	| Input port | Output port |
37	| --- | --- |
38	| `input` | `outcome-completed` |
39	
40	**The output port must be wired.** A node with no edge on `outcome-completed` blocks the flow indefinitely.
41	
42	### Output Variables
43	
44	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output` — object containing all output and inOut fields the human filled in
45	- `$vars.{nodeId}.output.{fieldName}` — individual field value
46	- `$vars.{nodeId}.status` — selected outcome's action value (`"Continue"` or `"End"`)
47	
48	### Schema Design
49	
50	The schema defines what the human sees and provides. Three field categories:
51	
52	| Category | Human can… | Use for |
53	| --- | --- | --- |
54	| `inputs` | Read only | Context the human needs to decide |
55	| `outputs` | Write | Data the automation needs back |
56	| `inOuts` | Read + modify | Fields the human can see and optionally correct |
57	
58	Outcomes are the action buttons (e.g., Approve/Reject). First outcome is primary.
59	
60	**In the architectural plan**, describe the schema:
61	```
62	inputs:   [invoiceId (string), amount (number)]
63	outputs:  [decision (string, required)]
64	outcomes: [Approve, Reject]
65	priority: Low
66	```
67	
68	Full JSON format and conversion examples: see [`uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill](../../../../../../uipath-human-in-the-loop/references/hitl-node-quickform.md).
69	
70	> **Note:** Skills are self-contained — cross-skill references are for documentation context only. The agent uses the `uipath-human-in-the-loop` skill to implement HITL nodes; this planning guide is for topology selection only.

73	
74	```
75	[Upstream] -> [HITL] ->|outcome-completed| [Continue]
76	```

79	
80	**Approval gate:**
81	```
82	Trigger -> Fetch Data -> HITL (review) ->|outcome-completed| Decision (approved?) ->
83	  true: Script (process) -> End
84	  false: Script (log rejection) -> End

18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "inputs": {

28	
29	See [Action Node Structure — Adding and editing procedures](../../../../shared/action-nodes.md#adding-and-editing-procedures). The script node uses the standard input port `input` and output port `success`; no plugin-specific wiring.

31	## Script rules
32	
33	1. **Top-level body — no `function main()` wrapper.** Node runs the `script` text directly (as a function body); a wrapper is never called → `output` null. Read workflow variables via `$vars.<variableId>` and upstream node outputs via `$vars.<nodeId>.output`; end with top-level `return {…}`. Not a coded Function: no `main`, no injected args.
34	   - Correct: `const n = $vars.ixp1.output.field; return { n };`
35	   - Wrong: `function main({ ixp1 }) { … }`
36	2. **Must `return` an object** — `return { key: value }`, not a bare scalar. The return value becomes `$vars.<nodeId>.output`.
37	3. **`$vars` is a global** — use it directly: `return { upper: $vars.customerName.toUpperCase() }`
38	4. **JavaScript ES2020 (Jint engine)** — see [variables-and-expressions.md](../../../../shared/variables-and-expressions.md) for supported features and Jint constraints.
39	5. **No `console.log`** — `console` is not available. Use `return { debug: value }` to inspect values.
40	6. **No external calls** — use the HTTP node or a connector node for API calls.
41	7. **30-second timeout** — long-running computations will be killed.
42	8. **Never name a variable `aggregate`** — reserved host global. On any `Identifier 'X' has already been declared`, rename `X`.
43	
44	**Script:** `python3 scripts/lint_jint.py <ProjectName>.flow` checks rules 1, 2, 5, 6 and 8 above (plus the wider unsupported-construct list) across every script node and `=js:` expression in the file. The 30-second timeout is a runtime property and is not statically checkable.

46	## Common patterns
47	
48	### Transform and return
49	
50	```javascript
51	const items = $vars.fetchData.output.body.items;
52	const filtered = items.filter(i => i.status === "active");
53	return { items: filtered, count: filtered.length };
54	```
55	
56	### Build a payload for a downstream node
57	
58	```javascript
59	return {
60	  subject: `Order ${$vars.orderId} - Confirmation`,
61	  body: `Your order of ${$vars.orderTotal} has been processed.`,
62	  recipient: $vars.customerEmail
63	};
64	```
65	
66	### Error check from upstream
67	
68	```javascript
69	const error = $vars.httpCall.error;
70	if (error) {
71	  return { hasError: true, message: error.message };
72	}
73	return { hasError: false, data: $vars.httpCall.output.body };
74	```

76	### Reading a file-typed variable
77	
78	A `file` variable (bound via `uip maestro flow debug --attachment <id>=<path>`) hydrates as an **object**, not a string. Read the uploaded file's name from `.FullName`:

80	```javascript

82	return { fileName: doc.FullName };        // .FullName, not .name/.fileName
83	```

352	| `binding` | **Input / inOut fields only.** Format: `"vars.<nodeId>.output.<field>"` for node outputs; `"vars.<globalId>"` for flow globals. **No `=js:$` prefix** — HITL binding is a raw path, not an expression. |
353	| `variable` | **Output / inOut fields only** — absent on input fields. Format: `"vars.<name>"` (always include the `vars.` prefix). Defaults to `"vars.<camelCase id>"` if not specified. |
354	| `required` | omit if false; set `true` for mandatory outputs |
355	| `outcomes[0]` | `isPrimary: true`, `action: "Continue"` |
356	| `outcomes[1+]` | `isPrimary: false`, `action: "End"` |
357	| `schema.schemaId` | Generate a fresh UUID (e.g. `crypto.randomUUID()` or any UUID v4) |
358	
359	### Example 1 — Simple approval (inputs only + outcomes)
360	
361	Business description: *"Reviewer sees invoice ID and amount, clicks Approve or Reject"*
362	
363	```json
364	"fields": [
365	  { "id": "invoiceid", "label": "Invoice ID", "type": "string",   "direction": "input", "binding": "vars.fetchData1.output.invoiceId" },
366	  { "id": "amount",    "label": "Amount",     "type": "number", "direction": "input", "binding": "vars.fetchData1.output.amount" }
367	],
368	"outcomes": [
369	  { "id": "approve", "name": "Approve", "type": "string", "isPrimary": true,  "action": "Continue" },
370	  { "id": "reject",  "name": "Reject",  "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" }
371	]
372	```
373	
374	### Example 2 — Write-back validation (inOut — human can edit before confirming)
375	
376	Business description: *"Human sees the AI-drafted email, can edit it, then clicks Send or Discard"*
377	
378	```json
379	"fields": [
380	  { "id": "recipient",  "label": "Recipient",  "type": "string", "direction": "input", "binding": "vars.draft1.output.recipient" },
381	  { "id": "emailbody",  "label": "Email Body", "type": "string", "direction": "inOut", "binding": "vars.draft1.output.body", "variable": "vars.emailBody" }
382	],
383	"outcomes": [
384	  { "id": "send",    "name": "Send",    "type": "string", "isPrimary": true,  "action": "Continue" },
385	  { "id": "discard", "name": "Discard", "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" }
386	]
387	```
388	
389	### Example 3 — Data enrichment (output — human fills in missing fields)
390	
391	Business description: *"Agent couldn't extract vendor name or cost center. Human fills them in and clicks Submit."*
392	
393	```json
394	"fields": [
395	  { "id": "rawextract",  "label": "Raw Extract",  "type": "string", "direction": "input",  "binding": "vars.extract1.output.rawText" },
396	  { "id": "vendorname",  "label": "Vendor Name",  "type": "string", "direction": "output", "variable": "vars.vendorName",  "required": true },
397	  { "id": "costcenter",  "label": "Cost Center",  "type": "string", "direction": "output", "variable": "vars.costCenter", "required": true }
398	],
399	"outcomes": [
400	  { "id": "submit", "name": "Submit", "type": "string", "isPrimary": true, "action": "Continue" }
401	]
402	```
403	
404	### Example 4 — Exception escalation (multiple outcomes + notes output)
405	
406	Business description: *"If agent confidence is low, escalate. Human sees reasoning and score, can Retry, Skip, or Escalate further."*
407	
408	```json
409	"fields": [
410	  { "id": "reasoning",       "label": "Agent Reasoning",  "type": "string",   "direction": "input",  "binding": "vars.classify1.output.reasoning" },
411	  { "id": "confidencescore", "label": "Confidence Score", "type": "number", "direction": "input",  "binding": "vars.classify1.output.score" },
412	  { "id": "notes",           "label": "Notes",            "type": "string",   "direction": "output", "variable": "vars.notes" }
413	],
414	"outcomes": [
415	  { "id": "retry",    "name": "Retry",    "type": "string", "isPrimary": true,  "action": "Continue" },
416	  { "id": "skip",     "name": "Skip",     "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" },
417	  { "id": "escalate", "name": "Escalate", "type": "string", "isPrimary": false, "action": "End" }
418	]
419	```
420	
421	> **`outcomeType` for middle outcomes:** Use `"Neutral"` when the outcome is neither clearly positive nor negative (e.g., Skip, Defer, Hold).
422	
423	---
424	
425	## Runtime Variables
426	
427	After the HITL node, downstream nodes can reference:
428	
429	| Variable | Type | What it contains |
430	|---|---|---|
431	| `$vars.<nodeId>.output` | object | All `output` and `inOut` field values keyed by **field `id`** |
432	| `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>` | varies | Individual field value using the field's `id` (e.g. `$vars.invoiceReview1.output.decision`) |
433	| `$vars.<nodeId>.status` | string | Selected outcome name (e.g. `"Approve"`, `"Reject"`) |
434	| `$vars.<globalId>` | varies | Workflow-global variable for output/inOut fields. `globalId` is `field.variable` with `vars.` stripped (e.g. `variable: "vars.notes"` → `$vars.notes`). **Do not use this path in scripts — use `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>` instead.** |
435	
436	> **`fieldId` not `variable`**: The output object properties are keyed by the field's `id` (e.g. `"decision"`), not by the `variable` property. The `variable` property (`"approvalResult"`) creates a separate workflow-global variable (`$vars.approvalResult`) — it does not change the key used in the output object. If a field has `"id": "dec1"` and `"variable": "vars.approvalResult"`, access it via the object as `$vars.nodeId.output.dec1`, or directly as `$vars.approvalResult`.
437	>
438	> **Common mistake:** A field with `"id": "approved"` and `"variable": "vars.legalApproval"` must be read as `$vars.<nodeId>.output.approved` — **not** `$vars.<nodeId>.output.legalApproval`. Using the `variable` name as the key produces `undefined` at runtime; `flow validate` does not catch it.
439	
440	**In a downstream script node** — always access inline using `$vars.<nodeId>.output.<fieldId>`, not by destructuring:
441	```javascript
442	// Correct — field ID inline access
443	const vendorName = $vars.invoiceReview1.output.vendorName;
444	const costCenter = $vars.invoiceReview1.output.costCenter;
445	if ($vars.invoiceReview1.status === "approve") {
446	  await updateSystem(vendorName, costCenter);
447	}
448	// Wrong — do NOT destructure first:
449	// const output = $vars.invoiceReview1.output;  // then output.vendorName misses the node path
450	```

1	# HITL Business Pattern Recognition Guide
2	
3	Use this guide to decide whether a business process needs a Human-in-the-Loop node, and where to place it — even when the user has not explicitly asked for one.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## When to Recommend HITL
8	
9	Look for these signals in the business description or process context:
10	
11	### Approval gate
12	The automation produces something that requires sign-off before it can proceed.
13	
14	| Signal phrases | Examples |
15	|---|---|
16	| "approve", "sign off", "authorize", "get approval" | Invoice approval, PO sign-off, budget authorization |
17	| "four-eyes check", "dual control", "maker-checker" | Financial transactions, compliance workflows |
18	| "review before posting", "validate before sending" | CRM updates, email campaigns, database writes |
19	
20	**Insertion point:** After the automation generates the artifact to review, before it takes the action requiring approval.
21	
22	---
23	
24	### Exception escalation
25	The automation hits a case it cannot resolve autonomously and needs a human decision.
26	
27	| Signal phrases | Examples |
28	|---|---|
29	| "if uncertain / low confidence, escalate" | AI agent confidence threshold |
30	| "edge case", "anomaly", "exception handling" | Fraud alerts, out-of-policy transactions |
31	| "escalate to manager / supervisor" | Customer service workflows |
32	
33	**Insertion point:** Inside a conditional branch where the automation detects it cannot proceed alone.
34	
35	---
36	
37	### Data enrichment
38	The automation extracted or generated data that is incomplete — a human must fill in the gaps.
39	
40	| Signal phrases | Examples |
41	|---|---|
42	| "fill in missing fields", "enrich", "complete the record" | Partially extracted invoice data |
43	| "human validates / corrects" | OCR output verification |
44	| "needs human input before continuing" | Missing vendor code, unknown cost center |
45	
46	**Insertion point:** After extraction/generation, before the downstream step that requires complete data.
47	
48	---
49	
50	### Compliance and audit checkpoint
51	A regulation or internal policy requires documented human sign-off.
52	
53	| Signal phrases | Examples |
54	|---|---|
55	| "compliance", "audit trail", "regulatory sign-off" | SOX controls, GDPR consent flows |
56	| "must be reviewed by", "requires attestation" | Legal review gates, privacy impact assessments |
57	
58	**Insertion point:** At the mandated checkpoint defined by the regulation or policy.
59	
60	---
61	
62	### Write-back validation
63	An agent or automation is about to write to an external system — a human must confirm the proposed change.
64	
65	| Signal phrases | Examples |
66	|---|---|
67	| "before writing to", "before posting to", "agent writes to ServiceNow / SAP / CRM" | Any write to a system of record |
68	| "human confirms before agent acts" | Autonomous agent guard rails |
69	
70	**Insertion point:** Immediately before the write/post action.
71	
72	---
73	
74	### Agentic output review
75	An AI agent produced a document, draft, classification, or recommendation — a human must verify it before the result is used or published.
76	
77	| Signal phrases | Examples |
78	|---|---|
79	| "review AI-generated content", "human verifies before sending" | Agent-drafted emails, RCA reports, meeting summaries |
80	| "check before publishing", "validate AI output" | AI-written case notes, support ticket responses |
81	| "human in the loop for AI decisions" | Any LLM output going to a system of record or customer |
82	
83	**Insertion point:** After the agent node, before the downstream action that consumes the output.
84	
85	---
86	
87	### IT / change management approval
88	A change request or access request needs human authorization before the automation executes it.
89	
90	| Signal phrases | Examples |
91	|---|---|
92	| "CAB approval", "change request", "change window" | IT change management (ServiceNow, Jira Service Management) |
93	| "access request", "provision access", "grant permission" | Identity and access management workflows |
94	| "runbook approval", "deployment sign-off" | DevOps release gates |
95	
96	**Insertion point:** After the automation prepares the change record, before it applies the change.
97	
98	---
99	
100	### HR and offer / contract workflows
101	A document or decision with legal or HR significance must be reviewed before it is sent to a third party.
102	
103	| Signal phrases | Examples |
104	|---|---|
105	| "offer letter", "employment contract", "onboarding approval" | HR hiring workflows |
106	| "termination review", "performance decision" | HR case management |
107	| "contract terms", "counter-sign", "legal review gate" | Procurement, vendor onboarding |
108	
109	**Insertion point:** After document generation, before the document is dispatched.
110	
111	---
112	
113	### Customer communication approval
114	An automation is about to send a message on behalf of a person or brand — a human must review tone, accuracy, or content before it goes out.
115	
116	| Signal phrases | Examples |
117	|---|---|
118	| "approve before sending", "review draft email", "check before posting" | Customer support responses, marketing emails |
119	| "agent-written reply", "draft response" | Helpdesk, CRM follow-ups |
120	
121	**Insertion point:** After the draft is generated, before the send/post action.
122	
123	---
124	
125	### Financial transaction approval
126	A monetary action above a threshold or of a certain type requires human sign-off.
127	
128	| Signal phrases | Examples |
129	|---|---|
130	| "above threshold", "over limit", "exceeds budget" | PO approval, expense reimbursement over limit |
131	| "wire transfer", "payment release", "credit note" | AP/AR workflows |
132	| "price override", "discount approval" | Sales quote approval |
133	
134	**Insertion point:** After the automation determines the transaction details, before it submits the payment or posts the entry.
135	
136	---
137	
138	## When NOT to Recommend HITL
139	
140	- The process description is fully automated with no decision point (e.g. "process all invoices automatically")
141	- The human interaction is asynchronous notification only (use email/Slack activity instead)
142	- The user explicitly says no human review is needed
143	- The decision can be made by a rule or AI model with sufficient confidence
144	- The user is asking about **runtime task management** — reassigning, monitoring, cancelling, or checking the status of existing Action Center tasks. These are operational questions answered by `uip tasks` commands or the Orchestrator UI, not by adding a HITL node. A question like "how do I reassign a task sitting for 3 days?" is task administration, not automation authoring — do not recommend adding a HITL checkpoint in response.
145	
146	---
147	
148	## Proactive HITL Recommendation
149	
150	If a business description contains any of the above signals but the user has not asked for a HITL, flag it:
151	
152	> "This process includes [signal]. Before the automation [action], a human should review [data]. I recommend inserting a HITL node here — want me to add it?"
153	
154	Then proceed to Step 3 (schema design) only after the user confirms.

1	# Action Node Structure
2	
3	Reference for the boilerplate shared by every action-node `impl.md` in this skill. Plugin docs should link here for the standard parts and only spell out what is plugin-specific: the registry type string, plugin-specific input fields, plugin-specific rules, debug entries, and node-type configuration workflows.
4	
5	## Registry validation
6	
7	Every action node should validate its registry contract before authoring:
8	
9	```bash
10	uip maestro flow registry get <node-type> --output json
11	```
12	
13	`registry get` returns the manifest at `Data.Node`. Do **not** inspect `Data` directly as if it were the node manifest.
14	
15	```json
16	{
17	  "Data": {
18	    "Node": {
19	      "nodeType": "core.action.script",
20	      "version": "1.0",
21	      "handleConfiguration": [
22	        { "position": "left", "handles": [{ "id": "input", "type": "target" }] },
23	        { "position": "right", "handles": [{ "id": "success", "type": "source" }] }
24	      ],
25	      "inputDefinition": {},
26	      "outputDefinition": {}
27	    }
28	  }
29	}
30	```
31	
32	Inspect:
33	
34	- `Data.Node.handleConfiguration` — input port name and output port name(s). Array of position groups, not a map with a top-level `handles` field.
35	- `Data.Node.inputDefinition` — required inputs.
36	- `Data.Node.outputDefinition` — downstream payloads.
37	- `Data.Node.model.serviceType` — where applicable.
38	
39	Plugin `impl.md` records what to confirm for that specific node type.
40	
41	## Standard JSON skeleton
42	
43	All action nodes share this base shape on the node instance:
44	
45	```json
46	{
47	  "id": "<nodeId>",
48	  "type": "<node-type>",
49	  "typeVersion": "<version>",
50	  "display": { "label": "<Label>" },
51	  "inputs": { /* plugin-specific — see plugin impl.md */ },
52	  "outputs": {
53	    "output": {
54	      "type": "object",
55	      "description": "<plugin-specific description>",
56	      "source": "=result.response",
57	      "var": "output"
58	    },
59	    "error": {
60	      "type": "object",
61	      "description": "Error information if the action fails.",
62	      "source": "=Error",
63	      "var": "error"
64	    }
65	  }
66	}
67	```
68	
69	`outputs.output` documents the success payload referenced downstream as `=js:$vars.{nodeId}.output`. `outputs.error` documents the failure shape; the runtime routes to the implicit `error` port when the action faults. See [Implicit error port on action nodes](file-format.md#implicit-error-port-on-action-nodes).
70	
71	> **For action nodes the instance `outputs` block is documentation, not the runtime contract.** What actually exposes the node's outputs as process-level `$vars.{nodeId}.output` is the matching `variables.nodes[]` entry — see [file-format.md — Node outputs](file-format.md#node-outputs). The BPMN emitter ignores the action-node instance `outputs` block at serialization (the manifest's `outputDefinition` drives the activity-side mapping). **Exception — Orchestrator-job nodes** (api-workflow, rpa-workflow, agent, agentic-process, function): the converter DOES read their instance `outputs` and copies each `source` verbatim, so a wrong `source` (e.g. `=result.response`) breaks `$vars.{nodeId}.output` — declare `error` only there. End / terminate nodes are also an exception: their instance `outputs` block IS consumed to map workflow-level `out` variables. `uip maestro flow format` regenerates `variables.nodes[]` from the current node graph (MST-9972), so running format after structural edits self-heals an omitted entry.
72	
73	## Standard ports
74	
75	| Direction | Common name(s) | Notes |
76	| --- | --- | --- |
77	| Input (target) | `input` | Every action node accepts a single input edge on `input`. |
78	| Output (success, source) | `output`, `default`, or `success` | Name varies by plugin — `registry get` is authoritative. |
79	| Output (error, source) | `error` | Implicit on every action node via `outputs.error`. |
80	
81	Some plugins add dynamic source ports (e.g., HTTP `branch-{id}` from `inputs.branches`); those are documented in the plugin's own `impl.md`.
82	
83	## Adding and editing procedures
84	
85	For step-by-step add, delete, and wiring instructions, see [editing-operations.md](../author/references/editing-operations.md) and the JSON recipes in [editing-operations-json.md](../author/references/editing-operations-json.md). Plugin `impl.md` files describe only the inputs and wiring patterns that are specific to the node type.
86	
87	## Migrating a plugin to reference this template
88	
89	When converting an existing plugin `impl.md` to use this template:
90	
91	- **Keep in the plugin:** registry type string, `typeVersion`, plugin-specific input fields, plugin-specific configuration workflow (e.g., `node configure` for HTTP/connector nodes), plugin-specific rules, common patterns, debug table.
92	- **Replace with a link here:** generic JSON skeleton, generic `outputs` block (`=result.response` / `=result.Error`), generic registry-validation prose, generic "Adding / Editing" cross-reference.

1 # Variables and Expressions 2 3 Complete reference for declaring variables, writing expressions, and managing data flow in `.flow` files. 4 5 > **Read this before** adding variables or writing expressions in any flow. 6 > 7 > `flow validate` catches the structural expression-reference errors: 8 > 9 > - Missing `=js:` prefix on `$vars`/`$metadata`/`$self` (MST-9107) 10 > - Invented `nodes..output` syntax 11 > - References to unknown variables or node IDs 12 > - Output-path walks that descend into declared primitives or schemas closed with `additionalProperties: false` 13 > 14 > Errors against **open output schemas** (HTTP response bodies, script returns, free-text agent output) and **wrong-direction reads** (e.g. reading an `out`-only variable) still slip past validate and surface only at `flow debug` or in production. 15 16 --- 17 18 ## Table of contents 19 20 - [Variables Overview](#variables-overview) 21 - [Workflow Variables (`globals`)](#workflow-variables-globals) 22 - [Node Variables (`nodes`)](#node-variables-nodes) 23 - [Variable Updates (`variableUpdates`)](#variable-updates-variableupdates) 24 - [Output Mapping on End Nodes](#output-mapping-on-end-nodes) 25 - [Expression System](#expression-system) 26 - [Available Globals](#available-globals) 27 - [Expression Contexts](#expression-contexts) 28 - [Jint Engine Constraints](#jint-engine-constraints) 29 - [Scoping Rules](#scoping-rules) 30 - [Variable Management via CLI](#variable-management-via-cli) 31 - [Complete Example](#complete-example) 32 33 --- 34 35 ## Variables Overview 36 37 Every flow has a `variables` object at the top level of the `.flow` file. It contains three sections: 38 39 ```json 40 { 41 "variables": { 42 "globals": [], 43 "nodes": [], 44 "variableUpdates": {} 45 } 46 } 47 ``` 48 49 | Section | Purpose | 50 | --- | --- | 51 | `globals` | Workflow-level variables: inputs, outputs, and state | 52 | `nodes` | Node output variables (auto-generated when using CLI `node add`) | 53 | `variableUpdates` | Per-node expressions that update state variables | 54 55 --- 56 57 ## Workflow Variables (`globals`) 58 59 Workflow variables are declared in `variables.globals`. Each has a **direction** that determines its role. 60 61 ### Directions 62 63 | Direction | Role | Readable | Writable | Use case | 64 | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | 65 | `in` | External input | Yes | No | Values passed when the flow is triggered or called | 66 | `out` | Workflow output | Yes | Mapped on End node | Values returned when the flow completes | 67 | `inout` | Internal state | Yes | Yes (via `variableUpdates`) | Counters, accumulators, flags shared across nodes | 68 69 ### Schema 70 71 ```typescript 72 { 73 id: string // Unique identifier, used in expressions as $vars.{id} 74 direction: "in" | "out" | "inout" 75 type?: string // "string" (default), "number", "boolean", "object", "array", "file" 76 subType?: string // Item type for arrays (e.g., "object", "string") 77 schema?: object // JSON Schema (draft-07) for complex types 78 defaultValue?: unknown // Initial value (must match type) 79 description?: string // Human-readable description 80 triggerNodeId?: string // Trigger node this input is associated with (works in both root flows and subflows) 81 } 82 ``` 83 84 ### Examples 85 86 **String input with default:** 87 ```json 88 { 89 "id": "customerName", 90 "direction": "in", 91 "type": "string", 92 "defaultValue": "Unknown", 93 "description": "Name of the customer to process" 94 } 95 ``` 96 97 **Number output:** 98 ```json 99 { 100 "id": "totalAmount", 101 "direction": "out", 102 "type": "number" 103 } 104 ``` 105 106 **State variable (counter):** 107 ```json 108 { 109 "id": "retryCount", 110 "direction": "inout", 111 "type": "number", 112 "defaultValue": 0 113 } 114 ``` 115 116 **Object with JSON Schema:** 117 ```json 118 { 119 "id": "orderData", 120 "direction": "in", 121 "type": "object", 122 "schema": { 123 "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#", 124 "type": "object", 125 "required": ["orderId", "amount"], 126 "properties": { 127 "orderId": { "type": "string" }, 128 "amount": { "type": "number" }, 129 "items": { 130 "type": "array", 131 "items": { "type": "object" } 132 } 133 }, 134 "additionalProperties": false 135 } 136 } 137 ``` 138 139 **Array with subType:** 140 ```json 141 { 142 "id": "emailList", 143 "direction": "in", 144 "type": "array", 145 "subType": "string", 146 "defaultValue": ["admin@example.com"] 147 } 148 ``` 149 150 **Input associated with a trigger:** 151 ```json 152 { 153 "id": "webhookPayload", 154 "direction": "in", 155 "type": "object", 156 "triggerNodeId": "start" 157 } 158 ``` 159 Accessed in expressions as `$vars.{triggerNodeId}.output.{id}` (the variable is nested under the trigger node's output — NOT `$vars.{id}`). 160 161 162 **File input (`type: "file"`):** 163 ```json 164 { 165 "id": "inputDoc", 166 "direction": "in", 167 "type": "file", 168 "description": "Document uploaded at trigger / bound via --attachment", 169 "triggerNodeId": "start" 170 } 171 ``` 172 173 > **Runtime shape of a `file` variable.** At runtime a `file` variable is an **object** (the *Flow Attachment* object), not a string. A Script node reading `$vars.start.output.inputDoc` receives: 174 > 175 > ```json 176 > { "ID": "", "FullName": "report.pdf", "MimeType": "application/pdf", "Metadata": { "size": "1024" } } 177 > ``` 178 > 179 > The uploaded file's name is **`.FullName`**. Property access is **case-sensitive** at runtime — these exact casings resolve, others return `undefined`/`null`: `.ID` (uppercase, not `.Id`), `.FullName`, `.MimeType`, and the **nested `.Metadata.size`** (lowercase `size`, NOT `.Size`). `.name` / `.fileName` do **not** exist. Two layers: the `.flow` *declaration* is camelCase (`type`, `direction`); the *runtime* object carries the casing above. Do NOT write `"FullName"` into the `.flow` source. Bind the file with `uip maestro flow debug --attachment =` — see [cli-commands.md — Pre-flight](cli-commands.md#attachment-preflight). 180 181 ### Type Reference 182 183 | Type | Default Value | Notes | 184 | --- | --- | --- | 185 | `string` | `""` | Default type if omitted | 186 | `number` | `0` | Integer or float | 187 | `boolean` | `false` | | 188 | `object` | `{}` | Use `schema` for structured objects | 189 | `array` | `[]` | Use `subType` for typed arrays | 190 | `file` | — | Bound at runtime via `--attachment`; hydrates as an object — read `.FullName` (see [File input](#file-input) above) | 191 192 --- 193 194 ## Node Variables (`nodes`) 195 196 Node variables represent outputs produced by nodes during execution. They are read-only and referenced via `$vars.{nodeId}.{outputId}`. 197 198 When you add a node via `uip maestro flow node add`, node variables are created automatically. When using `Edit` against the `.flow` file, add them manually. 199 200 ### Schema 201 202 ```typescript 203 { 204 id: string // Format: "{nodeId}.{outputId}" 205 type?: string // Output type 206 subType?: string // For complex types 207 schema?: object // JSON Schema for structured outputs 208 description?: string // What this output contains 209 binding: { 210 nodeId: string // Source node ID 211 outputId: string // Output port ID (e.g., "output", "error") 212 } 213 } 214 ``` 215 216 ### Example 217 218 ```json 219 { 220 "variables": { 221 "nodes": [ 222 { 223 "id": "fetchData.output", 224 "type": "object", 225 "description": "HTTP response body", 226 "binding": { 227 "nodeId": "fetchData", 228 "outputId": "output" 229 } 230 }, 231 { 232 "id": "fetchData.error", 233 "type": "object", 234 "description": "Error details if the request fails", 235 "schema": { 236 "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#", 237 "type": "object", 238 "required": ["code", "message"], 239 "properties": { 240 "code": { "type": "string" }, 241 "message": { "type": "string" }, 242 "detail": { "type": "string" }, 243 "category": { "type": "string" }, 244 "status": { "type": "integer" } 245 } 246 }, 247 "binding": { 248 "nodeId": "fetchData", 249 "outputId": "error" 250 } 251 } 252 ] 253 } 254 } 255 ``` 256 257 --- 258 259 ## Variable Updates (`variableUpdates`) 260 261 Variable updates assign new values to `inout` (state) variables at specific nodes. They execute when the node completes. 262 263 ### Schema 264 265 ```typescript 266 { 267 "variableUpdates": { 268 "{nodeId}": [ 269 { 270 "variableId": string, // ID of the inout variable to update 271 "expression": string // =js: expression to evaluate and assign 272 } 273 ] 274 } 275 } 276 ``` 277 278 ### Example 279 280 ```json 281 { 282 "variables": { 283 "globals": [ 284 { 285 "id": "counter", 286 "direction": "inout", 287 "type": "number", 288 "defaultValue": 0 289 }, 290 { 291 "id": "lastStatus", 292 "direction": "inout", 293 "type": "string", 294 "defaultValue": "pending" 295 } 296 ], 297 "variableUpdates": { 298 "processItem": [ 299 { 300 "variableId": "counter", 301 "expression": "=js:$vars.counter + 1" 302 }, 303 { 304 "variableId": "lastStatus", 305 "expression": "=js:$vars.processItem.output.status" 306 } 307 ] 308 } 309 } 310 } 311 ``` 312 313 > **Only `inout` variables can be updated.** Updating an `in` or `out` variable is invalid. 314 315 > **Inside loops:** variableUpdate expressions cannot access loop iteration variables like `$vars..currentItem`. Those are only available inside the body node's script. The variableUpdate must reference the body node's output (e.g., `=js:$vars.bodyNode.output`). 316 317 --- 318 319 ## Output Mapping on End Nodes 320 321 Workflow output variables (`direction: "out"`) must be mapped on End nodes. The End node's `outputs` object maps each output variable ID to a source expression. 322 323 ### Structure 324 325 ```json 326 { 327 "id": "end1", 328 "type": "core.control.end", 329 "typeVersion": "1.0", 330 "display": { "label": "End" }, 331 "inputs": {}, 332 "outputs": { 333 "totalAmount": { 334 "source": "=js:$vars.calculateTotal.output.amount" 335 }, 336 "summary": { 337 "source": "=js:$vars.formatResult.output.text" 338 } 339 } 340 } 341 ``` 342 343 > **Every `out` variable must have a mapping on every End node** that the flow can reach. Missing mappings cause runtime errors. 344 345 --- 346 347 ## Expression System 348 349 Flow uses a **Jint-based JavaScript engine** (ES2020 subset) for expressions. There are two expression formats. 350 351 ### `=js:` Expressions (Full JavaScript) 352 353 Used for conditions, input values, variable updates, and output mappings. The `=js:` prefix tells the engine to evaluate the rest as JavaScript. 354 355 ``` 356 =js:$vars.order.amount > 1000 && $vars.order.status === "approved" 357 ``` 358 359 ### Template Expressions (`{ }`) 360 361 Used for string interpolation in **native flow string fields** only. Expressions inside single braces are evaluated and converted to strings. 362 363 ``` 364 Order {$vars.orderId} is {$vars.status} — total: {$vars.amount} 365 ``` 366 367 > **Brace-templates do NOT work in Integration Service activity inputs.** The flow-layer template runner only processes native flow fields (decision expressions, variable updates, end-node output `source`, script bodies, agent prompt text). Fields inside `inputs.detail.bodyParameters` on `core.action.http.v2` or `uipath.connector.*` activity nodes — `url`, `headers`, `body`, `query` — are passed through to the IS runtime unchanged, so `{$vars.article}` ships literally. Observed behavior: the `$` is stripped and the braces survive (`user/{vars.article}` reaches the service). **For any dynamic value in an IS activity input, use `=js:` instead** — e.g., `` "url": "=js:`https://.../user/${$vars.article}`" `` or `"headers": { "Authorization": "=js:'Bearer ' + $vars.token" }`. 368 369 ### IS Activity Inputs Require `=js:` (Critical) 370 371 Every `$vars` / `$metadata` / `$self` reference inside `inputs.detail.bodyParameters`, `inputs.detail.queryParameters`, or `inputs.detail.pathParameters` on a connector or HTTP activity node MUST be wrapped with `=js:`. Without it the value ships as a literal string at runtime. 372 373 | Wrong | Right | 374 |---|---| 375 | `"recordId": "$vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | `"recordId": "=js:$vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | 376 | `"recordId": "nodes.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | `"recordId": "=js:$vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | 377 | `"recordId": "{vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id}"` | `"recordId": "=js:$vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | 378 | `"recordId": "=js:createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | `"recordId": "=js:$vars.createEntityRecord1.output.Id"` | 379 380 The serializer rewrites `$vars` → `vars` whether or not `=js:` is present, so a missing prefix yields a confusing failure: the runtime field is bound to the literal string `"vars.X.output.Id"` (which looks like an unevaluated expression).
